statements.claim: Once a year, the chief of the cowherds had business in the royal city; Nanda of Gokula made the journey to Mathura to pay the tribute his people owed the crown.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.18: Nanda travels to Mathura to pay the yearly tax; index summary 'annual tribute'.

statements.claim: He traveled plainly with a few attendants and bullock carts, a road he knew well.
statements.evidence: No detail of attendants/carts in pack; generic travel framing consistent with the yearly tax errand.

statements.claim: In Gokula, only days before, a son had been born to him, and the rejoicing had not yet cooled in his house.
statements.evidence: Pack does not date the birth; corpus chain previous story is 'Nanda Celebrates the Birth of His Son' (DKS_0020); recent birth consistent with BP 10.5.22 greeting in next episode.

statements.claim: Vasudeva heard that Nanda had arrived and rose at once from where he sat and went out to meet him, sending no one ahead.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.19-20: vasudeva upaśrutya bhrātaraṃ nandam āgatam / taṃ dṛṣṭvā sahasotthāya.

statements.claim: He threw his arms around Nanda and held him close, as though life itself had returned to his body, all the long waiting ended in that embrace.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.20: dehaḥ prāṇam ivāgatam ('as if life had returned to his body'); index summary: 'Vasudeva joyfully embraces him as a brother'.

statements.claim: They were not brothers by blood; Nanda was a cowherd chief and Vasudeva a man of standing in Mathura.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.18-19: Nanda is chief of Gokula's cowherds (gopān gokula-rakṣāyāṃ), Vasudeva a Mathura noble; 'brother' is the source's own address (bhrātaram).

statements.claim: For a long moment the two men stood together in the street; the tribute, carts and accounts could wait.
statements.evidence: Atmosphere/scene-setting; no counter-evidence in pack.

statements.claim: Nanda was moved by the warmth, having expected the city to be all business and no welcome.
statements.evidence: Internal reflection framing; not asserted in pack but not contradicted.

notes: Faithful to BP 10.5.18-20. The tribute errand, Vasudeva's sudden rising and life-returning embrace all match the Sanskrit; 'brothers' matches the source's bhrātaram address. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Vasudeva honored Nanda, seated him comfortably, and asked after his health with warmth.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.21: pūjitaḥ sukham āsīnaḥ pṛṣṭvānāmayam ādṛtaḥ.

statements.claim: Vasudeva said it was fortunate that Nanda, who for so many years had no child, now had a son to be the joy of his later years.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.22: diṣṭyā bhrātaḥ pravayasa idānīm aprajasya te.

statements.claim: The wheel of the world turns strangely; the friendship of dear ones does not stay fixed in a single spot, for each is carried by his own fortune.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.23-24: diṣṭyā saṃsāra-cakre 'smin vartamānaḥ punar-bhavaḥ / naikatra priya-saṃvāsaḥ suhṛdāṃ citra-karmaṇām.

statements.claim: He asked whether the cattle were free of disease and the water and grass plentiful; Nanda answered the herds were healthy and the pastures green.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.25: kaccit paśavyaṃ nirujaṃ bhūry-ambu-tṛṇa-vīrudham; Nanda's reply implied by his reassuring speech (10.5.28-29).

statements.claim: Vasudeva asked after his own two sons being raised in Nanda's care in Vraja, and after the mother who was with them.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.26: bhrātar mama sutaḥ kaccin mātrā saha bhavad-vraje.

statements.claim: A man's true wealth is not his goods but his friends, and through friends every aim a man holds in life is fulfilled.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.27: puṃsas tri-vargo vihitaḥ suhṛdo hy anubhāvitaḥ.

statements.claim: Nanda said the affairs of men are ruled by forces no one can fully foresee, and even a king's cruelty is the working of some unseen fate.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.28-29 (śrī-nanda uvāca): nūnaṃ hy adṛṣṭa-niṣṭho 'yam adṛṣṭa-paramo janaḥ — men are governed by the unseen; the kingly-cruelty gloss matches the fate-flavored original and index summary.

statements.claim: Vasudeva urged Nanda not to linger in Mathura, saying great disturbances and evil omens were rising in Gokula and would not wait for his return.
statements.evidence: Index excerpt (BP 10.5.21-32): 'tells him not to linger, for great disturbances are rising in Gokula'.

statements.claim: Nanda did not argue; he gathered his men, hitched their carts, and set out at once for Gokula.
statements.evidence: Index excerpt: 'Nanda and his men hasten back with their carts.'

notes: Faithful to BP 10.5.21-32. The seated greeting, the childless-years felicitation, the questions about cattle/water/grass and the hidden sons with their mother, the friends-as-wealth maxim, Nanda's fate speech, and the urgent warning all trace to the Sanskrit. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Kamsa, the king of Mathura, had not forgotten the child he feared; the prophecy had told him Devaki's child would one day take his life, and he had tried cages, guards and the sword.
statements.evidence: Not in the cited excerpt (BP 10.6.1-5); backstory framing from prior corpus episodes (Devaki prophecy, BP 10.1-4) consistent with kaṃsena prahitā in 10.6.1; not contradicted by the pack.

statements.claim: Putana was a demoness whose trade was children; wherever she went infants died, drawn to places where no protective hymn was chanted.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.1-2: pūtanā bāla-ghātinī / na yatra śravaṇādīni rakṣo-ghnāni sva-karmasu; index excerpt 'wandering among villages killing infants'.

statements.claim: She flew through the air from one settlement to the next, and one day rose into the air and turned toward Nanda's Gokula.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.3: sā khe-cary ekadotpatya pūtanā nanda-gokulam.

statements.claim: By her magic she took the form of a lovely woman — hair bound with fresh jasmine, waist slender, hips full, dressed in fine cloth, ears bright with ornaments, face framed in shining curls.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.4: keśa-bandha-vyatiṣakta-mallikā, bṛhan-nitamba-stana-kṛcchra-madhyamām, suvāsasaṃ, kalpita-karṇa-bhūṣaṇa, tviṣollasat-kuntala-maṇḍitānanām.

statements.claim: Her smiles and sidelong glances charmed the cowherd women, who took her for the goddess of fortune come to look upon her lord.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.5: valgu-smitāpāṅga-visarga-vīkṣitair mano harantīṃ vanitāṃ vrajaukasām; gopyaḥ śriyaṃ draṣṭum ivāgatāṃ patim.

statements.claim: The cowherd women welcomed her freely and showed her no suspicion; no one asked her name or turned her away.
statements.evidence: Implied by the gopis' being charmed and mistaking her for Śrī (10.6.5); not a separate asserted fact in the pack.

statements.claim: And somewhere in that village a child slept — the child Kamsa had sent her to find.
statements.evidence: Dramatic framing leading into the next episode (Putana's attack, BP 10.6.6-12); consistent with her mission (kaṃsena prahitā).

notes: Faithful to BP 10.6.1-5. The child-killing demoness, the protective-hymn detail, the flight into Gokula, and the full physical portrait (jasmine hair, full hips, slender waist, fine clothes, ear ornaments, curls) plus the Śrī-goddess mistake all match the Sanskrit. The prophecy backstory is prior-canon framing, not a fabrication. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Putana's body, released from the lovely form, lay where she had fallen — so vast that as she fell she crushed the trees for a long stretch around her.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.13: patamāno 'pi tad-dehas tri-gavyūty-antara-drumān ('crushing trees within three gavyūti').

statements.claim: Her mouth gaped wide with teeth like the shafts of a plow; her nostrils opened like mountain caves; her eyes were deep pits.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.14-15: īṣā-mātrogra-daṃṣṭrāsyaṃ, giri-kandara-nāsikam, andha-kūpa-gabhīrākṣaṃ.

statements.claim: The cowherds and their women trembled at the sight and none would draw near.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.16: santatrasuḥ sma tad vīkṣya gopā gopyaḥ kalevaram.

statements.claim: Krishna lay playing on the corpse's chest, utterly unafraid.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.17: bālaṃ ca tasyā urasi krīḍantam akutobhayam.

statements.claim: Yasoda and Rohini came forward and gathered him up.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.18: yaśodā-rohiṇībhyāṃ tāḥ samaṃ bālasya sarvataḥ.

statements.claim: The women bathed the child first with cow's urine and then with the fine dust of the cow pen.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.19: go-mūtreṇa snāpayitvā punar go-rajasārbhakam.

statements.claim: Touching and sprinkling water, they passed their hands over each part of him — feet, hands, waist, heart, throat, head — and chanted protective invocations over each.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.20-21: gopyaḥ saṃspṛṣṭa-salilā aṅgeṣu karayoḥ pṛthak; the body-part litany (aṅghri... kaṭi... hṛt... kaṇṭha... mukha) in verse 21.

statements.claim: They invoked the discus-holder before him, the mace-holder behind, the bow and sword at his sides, the conch above, Garuda on the ground, and the Lord of all everywhere around.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.22: cakry agrataḥ saha-gado harir astu paścāt / tvat-pārśvayor dhanur-asī madhu-hājanaś ca / koṇeṣu śaṅkha urugāya upary upendras / tārkṣyaḥ kṣitau haladharaḥ puruṣaḥ samantāt.

statements.claim: They named every spirit that preys on children and bade them stay far away.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.26-28: ḍākinyo yātudhānyaś ca kuṣmāṇḍā ye 'rbhaka-grahāḥ... pūtanā mātṛkādayaḥ... bāla-grahāś ca ye.

statements.claim: Meanwhile Nanda and the other cowherds were on the road back from Mathura; they reached the village to find the great body and the child safe, and marveled.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.30: tāvan nandādayo gopā mathurāyā vrajaṃ gatāḥ.

statements.claim: They said surely he was a great sage or a master of yoga, to have come through such a thing untouched.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.31: nūnaṃ batarṣiḥ sañjāto yogeśo vā samāsa saḥ.

statements.claim: They took up axes, cut the vast body to pieces, carried the pieces away and set them alight.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.32: kalevaraṃ paraśubhiś chittvā tat te vrajaukasaḥ.

statements.claim: As the body burned, the smoke carried a fragrance like aloe — sweet and clean — for the demoness had been granted the reward of a mother.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.33: dahyamānasya dehasya dhūmaś cāguru-saurabhaḥ; index summary: 'for she attained a mother's reward.'

notes: Faithful to BP 10.6.13-33. The crushed trees (three gavyūti), plow-shaft teeth, cave nostrils, well-deep eyes, playing infant, cow-urine/dust bath, full body-part protective litany, weapon-holders invocation, child-spirits list, Nanda's return from Mathura, axe dismemberment, and aloe-fragrant smoke all match the Sanskrit; the mother's-reward gloss is the index summary's own reading. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: On the day of a certain child's birth-rites in Gokula, a loaded cart overturned for no reason anyone could see, with only an infant near it.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.4-7: set during the autthānika ceremony; ano... śiśor alpa-pravāla-mṛdv-aṅghri-hataṃ vyavartata; kathaṃ svayaṃ vai śakaṭaṃ viparyagāt.

statements.claim: Yasoda, Nanda's wife, had bathed and purified herself; brahmins had recited benedictions over her newborn son and been honored with gifts.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.4: nandasya patnī kṛta-majjanādikaṃ vipraiḥ kṛta-svastyayanaṃ supūjitaiḥ.

statements.claim: The women of Vraja had gathered for the rite of the child's first rising, and Yasoda moved among them greeting each one.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.5: autthānikautsukya-manā manasvinī samāgatān pūjayatī vrajaukasaḥ; 10.7.7: autthānike karmaṇi yāḥ samāgatāḥ.

statements.claim: In the press of it all the child was set down for a moment in the shade of a cart heaped with vessels.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.6: adhaḥ-śayānasya śiśor ('the child lying beneath'); laden cart implied by the scattered vessels (10.7.6-7, Harivamsha 'pitcher... broken').

statements.claim: He began to cry and kicked; one small foot, soft and tender as a new leaf, struck the underside of the cart.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.6: alpa-pravāla-mṛdv-aṅghri-hataṃ (struck by the tender, coral-soft foot); Harivamsha: 'raising up his legs he overturned the carriage with one of them... began to cry for milk.'

statements.claim: The cart overturned violently — wheels wrenched from the axle, shaft and yoke broken, vessels spilled and shattered.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.6 vyavartata; Harivamsha 1.61: 'The axles, the pitcher and the rod were all broken'; index excerpt: 'its wheels and axle broken and its vessels scattered.'

statements.claim: The crash brought Yasoda, the women of Vraja, and Nanda and the other men running; they stood astonished, asking how a cart could turn over by itself, with no wind and no animal near.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.7: dṛṣṭvā yaśodā-pramukhā vraja-striya... nandādayaś cādbhuta-darśanākulāḥ / kathaṃ svayaṃ vai śakaṭaṃ viparyagāt; Harivamsha: 'without any wind... without the fighting of the bulls.'

statements.claim: The cowherd boys and girls said the child did it, kicked it with his own foot, but the grown men shook their heads, dismissing it as child-talk.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.8-9: ūcur avyavasita-matīn gopān gopīś ca bālakāḥ / na te śraddadhire gopā bāla-bhāṣitam ity uta; Harivamsha 1.61: boys said 'this boy upsetting the carriage with his feet'; the milkmen 'placed no confidence in the words of the boys.'

statements.claim: Yasoda was afraid of the evil eye and of unkind influence drawn to a child who had been part of such a wonder; she gathered up her crying son.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.10: rudantaṃ sutam ādāya yaśodā graha-śaṅkitā (fearing a grasping influence/graha).

statements.claim: The cowherds, strong men all, set the cart upright again and gathered up what remained of its goods.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.11: pūrvavat sthāpitaṃ gopair balibhiḥ sa-paricchadam.

statements.claim: Nanda had the protective rites recited over his son with the words of the three Vedas, and brought out his finest cows adorned with cloth, garlands and gold, standing with a steady heart while blessings were spoken.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.12-16: sāmarg-yajur-upākṛtaiḥ; vācayitvā svastyayanaṃ nanda-gopaḥ samāhitaḥ; gāvaḥ sarva-guṇopetā vāsaḥ-srag-rukma-mālinīḥ; viprā mantra-vido yuktās tair yāḥ proktās tathāśiṣaḥ.

statements.claim: The story follows the Bhagavata's placement of the episode during the birth-rites (not the Harivamsha's river-bathing setting), as disclosed in the tradition_note.
statements.evidence: tradition_note: 'The Harivamsha sets this episode while Yasoda is away bathing at the river... the Bhagavata Purana places it during the child's birth-rites'; story matches the Bhagavata setting.

notes: Faithful to BP 10.7.3-16 (primary), corroborated by Harivamsha 1.61 and Vishnu Purana 5.6. The birth-rites setting, tender-foot kick, shattered axle/yoke/vessels, everyone-runs astonishment, children's truth vs adults' disbelief, graha-fearing Yasoda, cart re-erection, and three-Veda rites with adorned cows all match. Variant-setting issue is correctly disclosed. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Yasoda sat with her son on her lap, dandling him and looking into his face.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.17: ekadāroham ārūḍhaṃ lālayantī sutaṃ satī.

statements.claim: Without warning the child grew heavy in her arms, so heavy she could hardly hold him; astonished, she set him down on the ground.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.18: bhūmau nidhāya taṃ gopī vismitā bhāra-pīḍitā.

statements.claim: A dry, violent wind tore through the lanes of Gokula, lifting dust and grit in a spinning wheel.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.20: gokulaṃ sarvam āvṛṇvan muṣṇaṃś cakṣūṃṣi reṇubhiḥ; 10.7.23: khara-pavana-cakra-pāṃśu-varṣe (fierce wind-wheel raining dust).

statements.claim: This was Trinavarta, a demon in the service of Kamsa, sent by his master in the shape of a whirlwind to do what the king could not.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.19: daityo nāmnā tṛṇāvartaḥ kaṃsa-bhṛtyaḥ praṇoditaḥ; index summary 'Kamsa's servant Trinavarta, in the form of a whirlwind, snatches the child away.'

statements.claim: The spinning dust filled the whole settlement and stole the light and sight of everyone in it; for a moment Gokula went dark and no one could see the person beside them.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.20-22: muṣṇaṃś cakṣūṃṣi reṇubhiḥ; muhūrtam abhavad goṣṭhaṃ rajasā tamasāvṛtam / nāpaśyat kaścanātmānaṃ paraṃ cāpi vimohitaḥ.

statements.claim: When the dust began to settle, Yasoda looked for her son and he was gone; she searched the spot and his path but the wind had scoured the ground clean, and she could not find him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.23: suta-padavīm abalāvilakṣya mātā ('the mother, unable to trace her son's path').

statements.claim: The other women of Gokula came running with tears on their faces, for the village's dearest child had been taken.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.24: ruditam anuniśamya tatra gopyo bhṛśam anutapta-dhiyo 'śru-pūrṇa-mukhyaḥ.

statements.claim: High above the blinded village the whirlwind rose with its small captive, believing it was carrying out the errand it had been sent on.
statements.evidence: Framing bridge to the next episode (Trinavarta crushed by the child's weight, BP 10.7.25-26, next in corpus chain); the demon's carrying the child off is implied by his mission and the mother's loss.

notes: Faithful to BP 10.7.17-24. The lap-dandling, sudden unbearable weight and setting the child down (bhāra-pīḍitā), Trinavarta as Kamsa's sent whirlwind-demon, the dust-darkened blinded goṣṭha, the unfindable path, and the tearful gopis all match the Sanskrit. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: It was the hour she fed her child — the child on her lap, nearly done with his milk, his drinking slowing.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.33-34: ekadārbhakam ādāya svāṅkam āropya bhāminī / pīta-prāyasya jananī sutasya rucira-smitam.

statements.claim: Yasoda looked down at his lovely, contented smile, and the child yawned.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.34 (rucira-smitam); index excerpt renders the opening mouth as a yawn: 'he yawns and she beholds within his mouth the sky...'

statements.claim: As his mouth opened, Yasoda saw within it the sky, the earth beneath, the heavens, hosts of stars, the directions, the sun and moon, fire and wind, the great oceans, and every living thing — the whole universe, moving and unmoving.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.35: khaṃ rodasī jyotir-anīkam āśāḥ sūryendu-vahni-śvasanāmbudhīṃś ca; index excerpt adds 'and all beings... the whole cosmos.'

statements.claim: She saw it suddenly and at once, and trembled, her limbs shaking and breath catching, understanding that the small mouth opened onto everything.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.36: sā vīkṣya viśvaṃ sahasā rājan sañjāta-vepathuḥ ('seeing the universe suddenly, trembling arose').

statements.claim: It lasted only as long as a yawn lasts; then the moment passed and he was only a child again.
statements.evidence: Scene pacing consistent with a brief glimpse; the pack does not specify duration, nor contradict it.

statements.claim: The source does not say how long she sat there afterward or what she said; it says only that she saw, and that she shook.
statements.evidence: Pack covers BP 10.7.33-37; no aftermath dialogue or duration is given in the excerpt.

notes: Faithful to BP 10.7.33-37. The nursing setting, the mostly-drunk child, the yawning mouth, the full inventory of the cosmos (sky, earth, lights, directions, sun, moon, fire, wind, oceans), and the sudden trembling all match the Sanskrit and the pack's rendered excerpt. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Krishna and his brother Rama grew quickly, and in a short time were crawling through the mud of the cowherd lanes, babbling as they went.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.20-21: kālena vrajatālpena gokule rāma-keśavau / tāv aṅghri-yugmam anukṛṣya sarīsṛpantau... vraja-kardameṣu; tan-nāda-hṛṣṭa-manasāv anusṛtya lokaṃ.

statements.claim: The people of the settlement were delighted by the sight and sound of the two boys.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.21: tan-nāda-hṛṣṭa-manasāv anusṛtya lokaṃ.

statements.claim: When they had crawled far enough they turned and crept back toward their mothers with puzzled, half-frightened faces, as if surprised to find themselves home.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.21: mugdha-prabhītavad upeyatur anti mātroḥ.

statements.claim: Their mothers gathered them up, pressed them to the breast, and looked into their faces with their sweet smiles and first little teeth, filled with joy.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.22: tan-mātarau nija-sutau ghṛṇayā snuvantyau... dattvā stanaṃ prapibatoḥ sma mukhaṃ nirīkṣya / mugdha-smitālpa-daśanaṃ yayatuḥ pramodam.

statements.claim: The boys caught the calves by the tail and let themselves be dragged about; the women of Vraja left their houses to watch, laughing.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.23: abalāḥ pragṛhīta-pucchaiḥ vatsair itas tata ubhāv anukṛṣyamāṇau / prekṣantya ujjhita-gṛhā jahṛṣur hasantyaḥ.

statements.claim: The two mothers tried to keep their sons away from horns, fire, a boar's tusks, open water, swooping birds and thorn bushes, and could not.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.24: śṛṅgy-agni-daṃṣṭry-asi-jala-dvija-kaṇṭakebhyaḥ... niṣeddhum... na śekāta.

statements.claim: Krishna and his band of cowherd friends slipped into a neighbor's house and set the calves loose at the wrong hour, laughing at the confusion.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.28: vatsān muñcan kvacid asamaye krośa-sañjāta-hāsaḥ.

statements.claim: He stole and ate sweet curd and milk with tricks and contrivances, choosing moments when the women were busy with housework.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.28-29: steyaṃ svādv atty atha dadhi-payaḥ kalpitaiḥ steya-yogaiḥ; kāle gopyo yarhi gṛha-kṛtyeṣu suvyagra-cittāḥ.

statements.claim: When pots hung high out of reach in slings among the rafters, he dragged a stool or a mortar beneath them and climbed.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.29: hastāgrāhye racayati vidhiṃ pīṭhakolūkhalādyaiś / chidraṃ hy antar-nihita-vayunaḥ śikya-bhāṇḍeṣu.

statements.claim: In the dark of a storeroom he needed no lamp, for the jewels on his small body caught the light and showed him where the pots were.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.29: dhvāntāgāre dhṛta-maṇi-gaṇaṃ svāṅgam artha-pradīpaṃ.

statements.claim: He shared the butter with the monkeys who were his audience, and if a monkey refused to eat he smashed the pot in a temper.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.28: markān bhokṣyan vibhajati sa cen nātti bhāṇḍaṃ bhinnatti.

statements.claim: When he could not reach a pot at all, he marched off angry and shouted curses at the little boys of the house.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.28: dravyālābhe sagṛha-kupito yāty upakrośya tokān.

statements.claim: The gopis complained to Yasoda with their lists of outrages, their anger undone by his lovely face, their scolding half-laughing; Yasoda, smiling, could not bring herself to scold him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.30: strībhiḥ sa-bhaya-nayana-śrī-mukhālokinībhir vyākhyātārthā prahasita-mukhī na hy upālabdhum aicchat.

notes: Faithful to BP 10.8.20-30. Crawling through Vraja's mud, mothers' joy over smiles and first teeth, calf-tail dragging, the horn/fire/tusk/water/bird/thorn dangers, calf-loosing, curd-and-milk theft, stool-and-mortar climbing, jewel-light in the dark storeroom, monkey-feeding and pot-smashing, cursing the house boys, and the gopis' complaint to a smiling, non-scolding Yasoda — all have direct Sanskrit antecedents. No unsupported or contradicted claims.
